bib.title: Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions", Roger Grosse*, Juhan Bae*, Cem Anil* (equal core contributors), Nelson Elhage, Alex Tamkin, Amirhossein Tajdini, Benoit Steiner, Dustin Li, Esin Durmus, Ethan Perez, Evan Hubinger, Kamile Lukosiute, Karina Nguyen, Nicholas Joseph, Sam McCandlish, Jared Kaplan, Samuel R. Bowman. Anthropic. arXiv:2308.03296v1, 7 Aug 2023. Preprint.

COVERAGE: Extraction OK (119 pages, 370,990 chars). I read all of it except the bulk of the long listings.
- Read in full: pp 1-61 (main text, Sec 1-6, Appendices A, B, C, D.1-D.4, Table 1) and the prose of D.5 (p61).
- Skimmed or skipped: pp 62-81 (D.5 and D.4 figure listings, Figs 36-41: long raw influential sequences; I read only the figure captions and intro text). Pp 82-87 (Appendix E, query listings, Figs 42-47): read the index paragraph plus the first listings (math_clips, math_earning). pp 88-109 (Appendix F, Surge crowdworker Tables 2-22): read Tables 2-6 and skimmed the rest via captions. Listing 1 (the crowdworker instructions) did not extract. pp 110-119 references: only searched for the origins, did not read.
- Figures with numeric data (Figs 6, 7, 9, 16, 17, 24-26, 30) are plots, and their values are not in the text. Only the quoted numbers below are available.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: EK-FAC approximates the inverse-Hessian-vector product about as accurately as the standard iterative method (LiSSA), is much faster, and scales influence functions to 52B parameters.
  number: "at least an order of magnitude less time"; models 810M to 52B
  setup: Pearson correlation with the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF, the "ground truth" here). Small tasks: UCI Energy and Concrete, MNIST, FashionMNIST (2-hidden-layer MLPs), CIFAR10 (ResNet-20), plus the 810M LM on 5 queries. 500 training points, averaged over 10 seeds. EK-FAC fitting cost is included in wall-clock time.
  quote: "EK-FAC achieves similar accuracy to the traditional iterative approach, but in at least an order of magnitude less time." (Sec 6). Also "EK-FAC is consistently competitive with LiSSA, despite being orders of magnitude faster when computing influences over several measurements (Figure 7)." (Sec 5.1)
  where: p1 abstract; p25; p50
- claim: Plain gradient dot product (identity in place of the Gauss-Newton Hessian) correlates worse with the PBRF than EK-FAC and LiSSA, so curvature matters. Its top sequences are unrelated to the query.
  number: 10 of top 50 vs 36 of top 50 (inflation query)
  setup: 810M model, 100,000 sampled training sequences, not a full scan
  quote: "for the inflation query, only 10 of the top 50 gradient dot product's influential sequences (compared to 36 for EK-FAC) contained keywords consumer price index, measure, or inflation which appear in the query."
  where: p60 (D.1); Fig 6 p24
- claim: Influence is heavy-tailed and sparse, but no single sequence explains an output. The authors read this as outputs coming from many sequences, not memorization.
  number: tail exponents alpha ~2.0-4.3; top 1% of sequences cover 12-52% of total positive influence; no influence above 1 nat
  setup: tail (top 0.01% of 5M unfiltered samples) fit by MLE; 8 queries on 52B for the power law, 22B for the top-1% figure; KS test (Table 1) rejects the power law for only 2 of 8 queries (objective p=0.01 and water p=0.01; the others have p from 0.10 to 0.92)
  quote: "for the 22B model, the top 1 percent of the sequences cover between 12 to 52 percent of the total influence for the queries we tested." and "influence values larger than 0.1 are rare, and none of the 8 queries visualized have any sequences with influence larger than 1." and "the standard deviation of the power law fit to the queries paperclips_large (α=2.1), shutdown (α=2.28) and water (α=2.57) is infinite"
  where: p25-27; Table 1 p61. The caption of Fig 8 shows alpha values slightly different from the text (e.g. shutdown 2.21 vs 2.28 in the text).
- claim: Larger models generalize more abstractly. Small-model top sequences share surface tokens with the query; 52B top sequences are thematically related (sci-fi about AI self-preservation, satire, code, math).
  number: none (qualitative; 810M, 6.4B, 22B, 52B)
  setup: queries shutdown, trade, inflation, neurosemantic_facutitious, math_clips, binary_search. Pretrained models (Kadavath et al. 2022 family), 512-token pretraining sequences, damping lambda = 0.1 x mean(eigenvalues of the layer).
  quote: "For an 810 million parameter model, all top 20 influential sequences share short token sequences with the query and are vaguely (if at all) semantically related. However, the top influential sequences for a 52 billion parameter model share little token overlap, but are related at a more abstract level."
  where: p5; 5.3.1 p28-34
- claim: Cross-lingual generalization grows with scale. English top-10 sequences have negligible influence on Korean/Turkish translations of the query at 810M, and increasing influence at larger sizes.
  number: none (shading plot, Fig 16)
  setup: top 10 English sequences for shutdown and water; queries translated by hand into Korean and Turkish
  quote: "For the smallest model, English training sequences have almost no influence on shutdown and water queries written in other languages. However, with increasing model scale, the cross-lingual influence of English sequences increases."
  where: p35 (Fig 16)
- claim: Influence is strongly sensitive to word order. A training sequence only influences a query if prompt-related phrases come before completion-related phrases. Flipping the order drops the influence by an order of magnitude or more.
  number: english_to_mandarin flip: 0.116 vs 0.030 (a Mandarin-only sequence scores 0.020); "at least an order of magnitude"
  setup: synthetic fictional facts ("first President of the Republic of Astrobia was Zorald Pfaff"; "Gleem is composed of hydrogenium and oxium") at 810M, 6.4B and 52B. Translation example on 52B. Influence functions only, not full training.
  quote: "when we flip the order of the English and Mandarin text in these sequences, the influence is reduced by at least an order of magnitude (and is possibly explainable as random noise for some)" and "The Mandarin-to-English sequence has an influence score of 0.030, which is similar to the score with a Mandarin-only sequence (0.020)."
  where: p41-46; Figs 24-27
- claim: Influence is spread roughly evenly across layers on average, but patterns differ by query type. Simple facts and memorized quotes sit in upper layers. Math, code and translation sit in middle layers. Restricting influence to the middle layers gives the most abstract sequences. A last-layer-only approximation would miss much.
  number: 50 queries x top 500 = 25,000 sequences; 9 layer blocks
  setup: 52B (810M is similar but less consistent, and unclear for math/code, App D.2)
  quote: "We computed the average layerwise influences from the top 500 influential sequences for 50 queries (a total of 25,000 influential sequences); as shown in Figure 17, for the 52B model, the influences were distributed nearly uniformly among the lower, middle, and upper layers of the network."
  where: p35-37; Figs 17-21
- claim: Role-playing behaviour (anti-shutdown, paperclips, superintelligent) traces to imitation of related text. The sequences are sci-fi, AI-risk articles and even a human survival story, not near-copies. The evidence is weak against the planning hypothesis, not conclusive.
  number: none
  setup: an early version of the Anthropic Assistant's outputs; influence computed on the pretrained models, not the fine-tuned Assistant. Models are smaller than the one that produced the responses.
  quote: "Our results provide weak evidence against the hypothesis that role-playing behavior results from sophisticated agent representations and planning capabilities, but we are unable to rule out this hypothesis directly."
  where: p47-50
- claim: Famous quotes are memorized, and influence scans find them. For the six quote queries, the top sequences contain the exact passage. For ordinary Assistant outputs, no clear copying was found.
  number: 6 queries
  setup: unfiltered scan with query batching; TF-IDF-filtered data for the general case
  quote: "We observed that invariably, the top influential sequences returned by our scan contained the exact famous passages."
  where: p41
- claim: Scanning cost. About 5M unfiltered sequences are estimated enough to match the top-10 influence from TF-IDF filtering. The authors scanned at least 10M. Rank-32 query-gradient compression loses almost nothing.
  number: ~5 million; >=10 million; rank 32, correlation 0.995 (shutdown); TF-IDF keeps the top 10,000 candidates (BM25, k1 = 1.5)
  setup: 52B for the Fig 3 correlation
  quote: "storing rank-32 approximations results in a negligible error in the final influence estimates, as shown in Figure 3" and "for most queries, we estimated that scanning about 5 million sequences would be sufficient (Figure 8). For the sake of comprehensiveness, we scanned at least 10 million sequences". The figure text gives "shutdown (Correlation = 0.995)".
  where: p19, p28; Fig 3
- claim: Block-diagonal approximation inside each layer cuts EK-FAC memory with a slight correlation drop. It was needed for the 52B model.
  number: block count O = 2 for 52B (O=2 halves covariance memory)
  setup: 810M tested on 5 queries (Fig 30); the percentages are in the plot only
  quote: "In this study, we use a block size of 2 (O=2) for the largest model investigated (the 52 billion parameter model)."
  where: App A, p52-53
- claim: Crowdworkers (Surge AI) judged a majority of the top sequences relevant. Some were irrelevant, and the paper marks highly sparse ones as probably spurious.
  number: 6 sequences x 7 queries per model size; sparsity flag when L2/L1 ratio of tokenwise influences > 2/3
  quote: "Overall, the crowdworkers found a majority of the most influential sequences to be relevant to their corresponding queries."
  where: p50, App F p88-109

LIMITS (as conceded)
- Influence functions are a poor match to the true counterfactual in deep nets (Basu et al. 2021). They are reinterpreted as approximating the PBRF (Bae et al. 2022a), which is local around the trained weights. Quote: "we therefore expect they would fail to capture important nonlinear training phenomena such as the formation of complex circuits". The authors do not test how well the PBRF captures real training effects. The Gauss-Newton Hessian is linear in the parameter-output map, so it cannot model induction-head-style coordination.
- Pretrained models only, not fine-tuning or RLHF. Models are at most 52B and smaller than the Assistant studied. Only MLP parameters are covered (attention, embeddings and layer norm are held fixed). Only a fraction of the corpus was scanned, so stronger sequences may be missed.
- TF-IDF filtering biases results toward token overlap. Query batching is unbiased but needs millions of sequences.
- Top-1% share is a crude measure, because it clips negative influence and so may overstate or understate concentration. Tokenwise signs are hard to interpret. A token's influence is not its counterfactual effect. The highlighted token is the one before the predicted token.
- Ground truth: no leave-one-out retraining (too expensive). PBRF was optimized with Adam, itself noisy for big models.
- The word-order result is shown through influence only. Nonlinear training may still generalize across orderings.
- Computing training gradients for candidate sequences is still the main bottleneck. Nearest-neighbour search is hard because (G+lambda I)^-1 whitens the space.
- Dated: this is 2023; later work on data attribution and on the reversal curse would postdate it.

BUILDS ON
- Koh and Liang (2017): imported classical influence functions into deep learning; iterative IHVP via LiSSA (Agarwal et al., 2017). Hampel (1974): the classical influence function from robust statistics. Quote: "influence functions, a classical technique from statistics (Hampel, 1974) imported into deep learning by Koh and Liang (2017)". Koh and Liang's cost: "possibly thousands of steps". Their own largest prior scale: "300 million parameter vision transformers (Schioppa et al., 2022)".
- K-FAC: Martens and Grosse (2015). EK-FAC: George et al. (2018), which fits diagonal eigenvalues in the Kronecker eigenbasis. Weight-sharing extensions: Grosse and Martens (2016, CNN), Martens et al. (2018, RNN).
- PBRF: Bae et al. (2022a), which gives the damped Gauss-Newton form. Damped GNH use: Teso et al. 2021. Gradient dot product baseline: Charpiat et al. 2019. Also Basu et al. 2021; Feldman and Zhang 2020 (single-layer influence is insufficient; self-influence as memorization); TracIn (Pruthi et al. 2020); Meng et al. 2022 (facts localized in MLPs). Power-law fitting test: Clauset et al. (2009). TF-IDF uses an Okapi BM25 variant (Ramos 2003).

CODE (verbatim equations worth keeping)
- Influence: "I_f(z_m) ≈ -∇θ f(θs)^T (G + λI)^-1 ∇θ L(z_m, θs)" (Eq 25, p16), with f(θ) = log p(z_c | z_p; θ) (Eq 24).
- EK-FAC damped IHVP: "(G + λI)^-1 v ≈ (QA ⊗ QS)(Λ + λI)^-1 (QA ⊗ QS)^T v" (Eq 21, p14), where Λ_ii = E[((QA ⊗ QS) Dθ)_i^2] (Eq 20), fitted with exact token-summed pseudo-gradients. Pseudo-gradient labels are sampled from the model, and the loss must be the sum over tokens (so that F = G).
- Layerwise decomposition: "I_f(z_m) ≈ Σ_ℓ q_ℓ^T (Ĝ_ℓ + λI)^-1 r_ℓ" (Eq 30), and tokenwise (Eq 31, p20).
- BM25 variant: score(Q,D) = Σ_t (k1+1)·exists_in_doc(t,D)/(k1+exists_in_doc(t,D)) · IDF(t), k1 = 1.5 (Eq 28).
- Spurious-sequence heuristic: tokenwise ||a||2/||a||1 > 2/3 (p28).

FIGURES (via text captions only; I did not run the figures script)
- Fig 1 (p7): shutdown query, top sequences at 810M vs 52B, tokenwise heatmap. The best single picture of "abstract with scale".
- Fig 2 (p11): influence functions as approximations of the PBRF, which explains why they are local.
- Fig 3 (p19): rank-32 compression, correlation 0.995.
- Fig 4 (p20): layer x token influence grid.
- Fig 6-7 (p24): correlation and wall-clock for gradient dot product, LiSSA and EK-FAC.
- Fig 8-9 (p26-27): power-law tails; top-1% share.
- Fig 16 (p35): cross-lingual influence vs scale.
- Fig 17-19 (p36-37): layerwise distributions.
- Fig 24-27 (p43-46): synthetic word-order ablations.

PROBLEMS
- Math symbols in the extraction are garbled (e.g. "‹", "θP RD"). I rebuilt the equations from context, so check them against the PDF before citing.
- Listing 1 (crowdworker instructions) is missing from the extraction.
- Text has no numeric values for Figs 6, 7, 9, 16 or 30, so I made no claims from them.
- Fig 8's alpha values differ slightly from the text (shutdown 2.21 in the caption vs 2.28 in the text).
- The page-count range for skimmed listings is given in COVERAGE above.
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF text.
